paragraphs.heading: Carbon as a clock
paragraphs.text: Radiocarbon dating, also called carbon dating or carbon-14 dating, finds the age of an object that contains organic material. It does this using radiocarbon, a radioactive isotope, or form, of carbon. The time it takes for half of a given sample to decay is about 5,730 years. Because of that, the oldest dates it can reliably measure are around 50,000 years ago, though special preparation sometimes allows accurate dating of older samples.

paragraphs.heading: Libby's idea
paragraphs.text: At some point during World War II, Willard Libby, then at Berkeley, heard of Korff's research and thought radiocarbon might be used for dating. Results summed up in a 1947 paper in Science suggested that materials containing carbon of organic origin could be dated. By contrast, methane made from petroleum, being so old, gave off no radiocarbon activity at all.

paragraphs.heading: Testing on known ages
paragraphs.text: Libby and James Arnold then put the idea to the test on samples whose ages were already known. Samples from the tombs of the Egyptian kings Zoser and Sneferu had been dated independently to 2625 BC ± 75 years, and radiocarbon gave an average of 2800 BC ± 250 years. These results appeared in Science in December 1949. Within 11 years more than 20 radiocarbon labs had opened around the world, and in 1960 Libby received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the work.

paragraphs.heading: The radiocarbon revolution
paragraphs.text: The method had a profound effect on archaeology, and histories of the field often call it the "radiocarbon revolution". It allows more accurate dating within a site than earlier methods, and it lets researchers compare the dates of events across great distances. Key turning points in prehistory have been dated with it, including when the last ice age ended and when the Neolithic and Bronze Age began in different regions.

paragraphs.heading: Why the sea looks old
paragraphs.text: The ratio of radiocarbon in the carbon exchange reservoir was once taken to be the same all over the world, but several causes of variation have since been found. Upwelling mixes old deep water with surface water, so the surface water has an apparent age of several hundred years, about 400 on average. The effect shifts by several hundred years even between nearby areas, and calibration software such as CALIB can correct for a sample's location. Shells and marine mammals such as whales and seals also give radiocarbon ages that look hundreds of years old.

paragraphs.heading: Hard water and dirty samples
paragraphs.text: In fresh water, the hard water effect, so called because it is often linked with calcium ions, which are typical of hard water, can give the water and the plants and animals living in it apparent ages of thousands of years. The effect varies so much that no general offset can be applied, and extra research is usually needed to size it. Contamination with old carbon causes an error the other way: a sample with 1% old carbon looks about 80 years older than it is, whatever its true date. Samples must first be treated to remove contamination, for example rootlets that grew into them after burial.
